formation.title: The Duchy of Silesia
formation.text:
The disparate Silesian duchies stand united at last under a single banner. For centuries this land has been divided among rival Piast branches, each petty duke guarding his patch of the Oder valley. Now the walled towns of Breslau, Schweidnitz, and Liegnitz answer to one authority.

But what kind of Silesia shall we build? Our duchy sits at the crossroads where Polish, Bohemian, and German cultures mingle, a place of many tongues and traditions, where Magdeburg law governs towns and Silesian linen reaches distant markets. Shall we embrace this diversity as our defining strength, governing through diplomacy and multi-ethnic tolerance? Or shall we look to the looms and mineshafts that have always been the true source of Silesian wealth, building an industrial heartland that rivals Flanders and Saxony?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: We are the bridge between three kingdoms.

modifiers.name: Crossroads of Three Crowns
modifiers.text: Silesia has long stood at the intersection of Polish, Bohemian, and German worlds. Rather than being torn apart by these competing claims, we have made our multi-ethnic heritage a source of strength, welcoming settlers, mediating disputes, and governing through compromise.

options.text: Our wealth is woven in cloth and dug from stone.

modifiers.name: The Linen and Silver Land
modifiers.text: The wealth of Silesia flows from the looms of its weavers and the depths of its mines. Our linen cloth reaches the markets of Amsterdam and London, while Silesian silver and lead fuel the mints of Central Europe. This is a land built on industry and enterprise.

advances.name: Piast Fortifications
advances.text: The Silesian Piast dukes raised stone strongholds across their duchies, from Wroclaw's castle to the hill forts of the Sudeten foothills, creating a network of defensive positions against Mongol, Hussite, and rival claimants alike.

advances.name: Legacy of Legnica
advances.text: The Battle of Legnica in 1241 defined Silesia's martial identity. Duke Henry the Pious's cavalry charge against the Mongol vanguard, though doomed, demonstrated the Piast tradition of mounted warfare that characterized Silesian military culture.

event.title: The Shadow of Legnica
event.text:
In the spring of 1241, the Mongol tumens swept through Silesia like a brushfire. At Legnica, Duke Henry II the Pious gathered what forces he could, Silesian knights, Templar brothers, Bavarian miners turned soldiers, and rode out to meet the horde. The battle was a catastrophe. Henry was killed, his head paraded on a Mongol lance. Yet the Mongols did not stay. Whether turned back by their losses or called east by the death of the Great Khan, they withdrew, leaving Silesia devastated but unconquered.

The memory of Legnica burns in Silesian consciousness. Shall we honor Henry's sacrifice by hardening our defenses so thoroughly that no invader will ever breach them again? Or shall we make the martyred duke a symbol of our eternal defiance, a rallying cry that draws warriors and pilgrims alike to our banner?

modifiers.name: Resilience of Legnica
modifiers.text: The memory of Duke Henry the Pious and his sacrifice against the Mongol horde steels our defenders. What was destroyed has been rebuilt stronger.

modifiers.name: Martyrdom of Henry the Pious
modifiers.text: Duke Henry's death at Legnica made him a Christian martyr and a symbol of Silesian defiance. His sacrifice brought pilgrims, prestige, and renewed devotion to our land's defense.

advances.name: Oder River Commerce
advances.text: The River Oder forms the commercial spine of Silesia, carrying grain, timber, and cloth downstream to the Baltic ports and bringing salt, herring, and foreign luxuries upstream to Breslau's bustling markets.

advances.name: Silesian Magdeburg Law
advances.text: The Piast dukes invited German settlers to Silesia under Magdeburg law, granting towns self-governance, market rights, and judicial independence. This legal framework transformed Silesian settlements into prosperous urban centers.

advances.name: Piast Fragmentation
advances.text: The division of Silesia among rival Piast branches, at one point numbering seventeen separate duchies, bred a peculiar political culture: endless negotiation, flexible allegiances, and a talent for managing diversity that served Silesia well under larger empires.

advances.name: Silesian Linen Weaving
advances.text:
From the sixteenth century onward, Silesian linen became a prized commodity across Europe. Village weavers in the Sudeten foothills produced cloth that rivaled Flemish and Irish linen, exported through merchant networks to markets as far as the Americas.

Available in: Silesian Linen Workshop

advances.name: Urban Militia Tradition
advances.text: The walled towns of Silesia maintained citizen militias armed with crossbows and later handguns. These burghers defended their market privileges with the same tenacity they applied to commerce, forming a reliable urban defense force.

advances.name: Breslau Emporium
advances.text: Breslau sat astride the junction of the Amber Road and the Via Regia, making it one of Central Europe's great trading cities. Its cloth halls, salt markets, and commodity exchanges connected the Baltic to the Mediterranean. The dark beer of Schweidnitz has been drawn in the cellar beneath its town hall since 1273.

advances.name: Hussite Defenses
advances.text: The devastating Hussite raids of the 1420s and 1430s, which destroyed over thirty Silesian towns, forced a comprehensive rebuilding of urban fortifications. Stone walls, reinforced gates, and permanent garrisons became standard across the duchy.

advances.name: Crown Land Administration
advances.text: When Silesia passed to the Bohemian Crown in 1335 and later to the Habsburgs, its governance was reorganized under centralized administrative systems that brought fiscal efficiency and legal uniformity to the formerly fragmented duchy.

advances.name: Silver and Lead Mines
advances.text: The mountains of Upper Silesia yielded rich deposits of silver and lead, worked by skilled miners using increasingly sophisticated techniques. Tarnowitz and other mining towns became centers of metallurgical expertise.

advances.name: Oder Trade Network
advances.text: Breslau's position on the Oder River, combined with its membership in the Hanseatic League, created a vast trade network linking Silesian cloth and mineral wealth to Baltic commerce, Bohemian markets, and Italian banking houses.

advances.name: Silesian Landsknechte
advances.text: Silesian towns contributed disciplined pike-and-shot infantry to Imperial armies, drawing on the German military tradition of the Landsknechte. These professional soldiers brought the latest tactical innovations to Silesian warfare.

advances.name: Three Crown Diplomacy
advances.text: Silesia's position between the Polish, Bohemian, and Imperial crowns demanded exceptional diplomatic skill. Silesian dukes and town councils became adept at playing one overlord against another, extracting privileges through careful negotiation.

advances.name: Silesian Printing Press
advances.text: The introduction of printing to Breslau in the late fifteenth century catalyzed Silesian intellectual life. Protestant tracts, scholarly works, and commercial records flowed from Silesian presses, making the duchy a center of Central European learning.

advances.name: Breslau Reformation
advances.text: Johann Hess's appointment in 1523 transformed Breslau into an eastern bastion of Protestantism. The city's churches converted en masse, and Silesia became one of the most religiously contested territories in the Empire.

event.title: The Reformation in Breslau
event.text:
In 1523, the Breslau town council unanimously appointed Johann Hess, a student of Wittenberg and close friend of Melanchthon, as pastor of St. Maria Magdalena. Within a few years, nearly every church in Breslau turned Protestant, save the ancient cathedral on its island. The city became a beacon of the Reformation in the east, drawing scholars and preachers from across the Empire.

Yet Silesia's religious geography is complex. Catholic orders still hold their monasteries, Schwenckfelder mystics preach in the countryside, and the Habsburg overlords eye this Protestant surge with growing alarm. Shall we embrace the Reformation with evangelical zeal, making Breslau a fortress of the new faith? Or shall we follow the Silesian instinct for accommodation, letting Protestant and Catholic, mystic and rationalist, coexist in a land that has always thrived on diversity?

options.text: Breslau shall be a city of the true faith.

modifiers.name: Silesian Protestant Fervor
modifiers.text: The Reformation has swept through Breslau's churches with the passion of true conviction. Johann Hess's sermons echo in every parish, and the faithful look to Silesia as a bastion of the new faith.

options.text: Let all who seek truth find welcome here.

modifiers.name: Silesian Religious Pluralism
modifiers.text: In a land where Catholic Cathedral Island and Protestant merchant quarters share the same city, Silesia has learned that coexistence breeds prosperity. Our scholars debate freely and our traders welcome all.

advances.name: Silesian Mountain Jaegers
advances.text: The forested mountains of the Sudeten range bred skilled hunters and woodsmen who, trained in skirmish tactics, became effective light infantry. These Silesian Jaegers excelled at ambush and irregular warfare in broken terrain.

advances.name: Linen Export Boom
advances.text: By the seventeenth century, Silesian linen dominated European markets. Merchants from Schweidnitz organized purchase networks reaching every cottage loom in the mountain villages, while export agents shipped cloth to Holland, England, Spain, and their colonial empires. The same valleys send out cut glass from the forest huts of the Schaffgotsch lands.

advances.name: Habsburg Governance
advances.text: Under Habsburg administration from 1526, Silesia was incorporated into the complex bureaucratic machinery of the Austrian Monarchy. Imperial officials, tax collectors, and legal reforms brought centralized governance to the formerly autonomous principalities.

advances.name: Silesian Religious Coexistence
advances.text: The Treaty of Altranstadt in 1707 secured Protestant worship rights in Silesia, codifying a tradition of religious coexistence that had deep roots in the duchy's multi-ethnic character. Catholic, Protestant, and Schwenckfelder communities learned to share the same valleys. The three Churches of Peace at Glogau, Jauer and Schweidnitz, raised in timber before the town walls after 1648, are its monuments.

advances.name: Upper Silesian Coal
advances.text: The vast coal deposits of Upper Silesia began to be systematically exploited in the late eighteenth century, powered by the first steam engines in the region. This black wealth would transform Silesia into one of Central Europe's great industrial zones.

advances.name: Silesian Fusilier Tradition
advances.text: The Silesian Wars between Prussia and Austria made the duchy a crucible of military innovation. Silesian regiments, drilled in the Frederician system, became some of the finest line infantry in Europe.

advances.name: Breslau University
advances.text: The Jesuit university founded in 1702, and its later merger with the Protestant Viadrina in 1811, created a powerhouse of learning that attracted scholars from across the German-speaking world.

advances.name: Contested Borderland
advances.text: The three Silesian Wars between Frederick the Great and Maria Theresa made the duchy Europe's most fought-over territory. This constant militarization forged a hardened populace accustomed to the demands of war.

advances.name: Silesian Linen Monopoly
advances.text:
At its peak, Silesian linen was exported to England, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Portugal, Scandinavia, Russia, Turkey, and even the markets of Africa and the Americas, a proto-industrial achievement rivaling any in Europe. The finest of it was the white veil linen of Hirschberg, bleached on the valley meadows and sold by the merchant lords of the town.

Available in: Silesian Linen Workshop

advances.name: Industrial Silesia
advances.text: The mechanization of Silesian industry, steam-powered looms replacing cottage weavers, coal-fired furnaces replacing charcoal, transformed the duchy into one of the great industrial regions of nineteenth-century Europe.

advances.name: Weavers' Revolt
advances.text: The desperate uprising of Silesian linen weavers in 1844, crushed by Prussian troops, became a symbol of the human cost of industrialization and inspired generations of social reformers and labor organizers.

event.title: The Silesian Weavers' Uprising
event.text:
In the hill country around Peterswaldau and Langenbielau, the linen weavers have risen in desperate fury. For generations these cottage workers were the backbone of Silesian prosperity, their cloth exported to England, the Netherlands, and the distant colonies. But mechanized competition from British factories has driven prices into the ground, while merchants squeeze ever harder. The weavers, reduced to starvation wages, have smashed the merchants' houses and destroyed their account books.

The uprising has been put down by Prussian troops, but the underlying tension remains. Shall we make concessions to the working poor, better wages, regulated conditions, accepting that a content workforce is a productive one? Or shall we restore order with an iron hand, ensuring that Silesian industry maintains its discipline and its competitive edge in the global marketplace?

options.text: Grant the weavers dignity, and they will weave with pride.

modifiers.name: Weavers' Compact
modifiers.text: The uprising of the Silesian weavers has forced our hand, but concessions to the laboring poor may yet prove the wiser path. A satisfied workforce weaves faster and better.

options.text: The looms of Silesia shall not be stilled by disorder.

modifiers.name: Industrial Order
modifiers.text: The weavers' revolt has been crushed. Order must be maintained in the workshops, and the looms must not fall silent. Silesian cloth will continue to reach every market in Europe.

advances.name: Silesian Iron and Steel
advances.text:
Upper Silesia's combination of coal, iron ore, and zinc deposits created a heavy industrial complex that rivaled the Ruhr. Steelworks and foundries transformed the landscape and drew workers from across Central Europe.

Available in: Silesian Coal Works

advances.name: Enlightened Breslau
advances.text: Breslau's salons, theaters, and publishing houses made it one of the cultural capitals of eastern Germany. The city nurtured poets, philosophers, and scientists who contributed to the broader Enlightenment.

advances.name: Silesian National Awakening
advances.text: The nineteenth century brought competing Polish and German national movements to Silesia, each claiming the duchy's heritage. This awakening of national consciousness reshaped Silesian identity and its relationship with neighboring states.

destiny.name: Silesian Destiny
destiny.text: United Silesia stands ready to chart its course. The fractured Piast duchies have been forged into a single state, and now the question is what kind of power Silesia will become.

event.title: The Silesian Destiny
event.text: The duchy stands united and our course is set. Whether through diplomacy between crowns or the wealth of looms and mineshafts, Silesia shall rise to its full potential. The traditions of the Piast dukes, their fortitude, their enterprise, their talent for governing diversity, shall carry us forward into a new era.

destiny.name: The Polish Crown
destiny.text: Silesia's oldest ties run south and east to Krakow, seat of the Piast kings who once ruled these lands. To prove ourselves as a bridge between kingdoms, we must first reclaim the city where Silesian and Polish history began.

event.title: Krakow Falls to Silesian Arms
event.text:
The ancient capital of the Piast kings now flies the Silesian banner. Krakow, where Boleslaw the Brave was crowned and where generations of Polish monarchs held court, has passed under our authority. It is a potent symbol, the branch of the Piast dynasty that ruled Silesia has now reclaimed the seat of its ancestors.

The Polish crown, once Silesia's overlord, must now reckon with a Silesian state that controls the headwaters of both the Oder and the Vistula.

destiny.name: The Bohemian Crown
destiny.text: Prague beckons. The Bohemian Crown has claimed Silesia since 1335, and now we shall reverse that relationship. Take the golden city and build it up further, and Central European politics shall bend to Silesian diplomacy.

conditions.text: We own Prague and its development is at least 54

event.title: Prague Under Silesian Suzerainty
event.text:
Two of the three crowns are ours. Prague, the golden city on the Moldau, whose Bohemian kings once summoned Silesian dukes to pay homage, now answers to Breslau. The reversal is extraordinary, from vassal to overlord in the span of generations.

With Prague comes its chancery, its banking houses, and its centuries of administrative tradition. Shall we absorb the Bohemian bureaucratic apparatus to run our growing realm with precision? Or shall we embrace the martial legacy of the Hussite wars, drawing on Bohemia's proven military traditions to forge an army that can challenge any power in Central Europe?

modifiers.name: Bohemian Chancellery
modifiers.text: The administrative apparatus of the Bohemian crown has been integrated into Silesian governance, bringing centuries of bureaucratic expertise to our growing realm.

modifiers.name: Hussite Military Legacy
modifiers.text: The martial traditions of the Hussite wars have been absorbed into Silesian military doctrine. Wagon forts, aggressive siege tactics, and the fighting spirit of Zizka's heirs strengthen our armies.

destiny.name: The Imperial Crown
destiny.text: Vienna, seat of the Habsburgs and the Imperial Diet, is the ultimate prize. Only by placing all three crown cities under Silesian authority can we fulfill the destiny of the crossroads state, not a subject of empires, but their arbiter.

event.title: Arbiter of Three Crowns
event.text:
Vienna is ours. The seat of Habsburg power, the capital of the Holy Roman Empire, the city that has dictated Central European politics for centuries, all under the Silesian banner. From Krakow to Prague to Vienna, the three crowns that once competed for control of Silesia now answer to it.

This is unprecedented. A duchy once divided among seventeen petty princes has become the paramount power of Central Europe. Shall we use this position to become the Empire's supreme arbitrator, settling disputes from the Baltic to the Adriatic through diplomacy? Or shall we embrace the reality of our new power and forge a Central European hegemony backed by overwhelming military might?

options.text: We shall be the Empire's just arbiter.

modifiers.name: Imperial Arbitrator
modifiers.text: Silesia's control of all three crown cities makes it the natural arbiter of Central European disputes. Our diplomats settle conflicts from the Baltic to the Alps.

options.text: Central Europe bows to Silesian might.

modifiers.name: Central European Hegemon
modifiers.text: The combined manpower and resources of three kingdoms sustain a military establishment that no Central European power can challenge. Silesian hegemony is maintained by the sword.

destiny.name: Bohemian Silver
destiny.text: The legendary silver mines of Kutna Hora have bankrolled Bohemian kings for centuries. Extending Silesian control over these mines would unite the richest mining districts in Central Europe under one administration.

event.title: The Mines of Kutna Hora
event.text:
Silesian miners now work alongside their Bohemian counterparts in the legendary silver mines of Kutna Hora. For centuries, the groschen minted from this silver financed Bohemian kings and paid Imperial armies. Now that wealth flows through Silesian banks and Silesian counting houses.

Combined with our own mines at Tarnowitz and Zlotoryja, Silesia now controls the richest mineral belt in Central Europe. The looms and the mines, the twin pillars of Silesian prosperity, grow stronger together.

options.text: Silver from Bohemia, linen from Silesia.

destiny.name: Baltic Trade
destiny.text: The Oder carries our linen north, but the Baltic trade is dominated by Lubeck and its Hanseatic partners. To become a true commercial power, Silesia must seize Lubeck and Stettin at the mouth of the Oder, and control the entire chain from loom to ship.

event.title: Silesian Ships in Lubeck Harbor
event.text:
The great Hanseatic port of Lubeck answers to Silesia. For the first time, the linen and minerals that flow down the Oder need not pass through middlemen to reach the Atlantic markets; our own merchants control the entire chain from workshop to wharf.

Shall we claim the old Hanseatic trading privileges for ourselves, opening our markets to the free flow of Baltic commerce? Or shall we exploit our monopoly over the Oder shipping route, taxing every bale of cloth and barrel of goods that passes between Silesia and the sea?

modifiers.name: Hanseatic Privileges
modifiers.text: The old Hanseatic trading rights and market privileges now serve Silesian merchants, opening the ports of the Baltic to our linen, minerals, and manufactured goods.

modifiers.name: Oder Shipping Monopoly
modifiers.text: Control of the entire Oder waterway from source to sea gives Silesia a stranglehold on Central European north-south commerce. Every merchant pays the Silesian toll.

destiny.name: Industrial Heartland
destiny.text: Leipzig's trade fairs draw merchants from across Europe. Combined with Silesian coal, iron, and linen, control of this commercial hub would make our industrial heartland the workshop of Central Europe. Breslau itself is to be built up into a great city.

conditions.text: We own Breslau and its development is at least 52

Cloth is traded in the market

event.title: The Workshop of Central Europe
event.text:
Leipzig's great trade fairs, the Michaelmas Fair, the Easter Fair, the New Year Fair, now serve as the showroom for Silesian industry. Coal from Upper Silesia fires the furnaces, iron feeds the forges, and linen drapes the stalls. Our industrial heartland stretches from the Sudeten mountains to the Saxon plain.

This is the apex of the Silesian economic miracle. Shall we entrust this vast industrial complex to the factory owners and mine operators, letting their capital and ambition drive relentless growth? Or shall we foster a spirit of merchant enterprise, keeping commerce open, credit cheap, and markets competitive?

options.text: Let the factory lords lead our growth.

modifiers.name: Factory Lords
modifiers.text: The great industrialists of Upper Silesia drive relentless expansion, building factories, sinking mines, and drawing workers from across Central Europe. Growth comes at the price of social complacency.

options.text: Commerce and enterprise shall be our way.

modifiers.name: Merchant Republic Spirit
modifiers.text: The old Breslau tradition of merchant self-governance has been extended across the Silesian industrial heartland. Cheap credit, mercenary protection, and liberal commerce fuel sustained prosperity.

units.name: Silesian Piast Lancers
units.text: Light cavalry descended from the Piast ducal retinues, skilled at raiding and reconnaissance across the Oder valley.

units.name: Silesian Crossbowmen
units.text: Burgher militia armed with crossbows, drawn from the fortified towns of Breslau, Schweidnitz, and Liegnitz.

units.name: Silesian Jaegers
units.text: Light infantry skirmishers recruited from the hunters and woodsmen of the Sudeten mountain forests. They shoot first and aim well, and do not stand a charge.

units.name: Silesian Fusiliers
units.text: Line infantry drilled in the exacting traditions of Frederick's Silesian campaigns, steady under fire and precise in volley.

buildings.name: Silesian Ducal Stronghold
buildings.text: A fortified residence of the Piast dukes, combining administrative center with military garrison. These strongholds anchored Silesian defense against Mongol, Hussite, and rival incursions.

buildings.name: Silesian Linen Workshop
buildings.text: A weaving workshop producing fine Silesian linen cloth for export. Village looms and urban finishing houses work together to create textiles prized across European markets.

buildings.name: Schweidnitz Brewhouse
buildings.text: A town brewhouse of the kind that made Schweidnitz known: dark strong beer, brewed by right of the town charter and carted to the cellars of Breslau.

buildings.name: Silesian Mining Pit
buildings.text: Shafts, pit props and drainage adits on the silver and lead fields of Silesia, worked by skilled miners with ever deeper techniques. The pit raises the silver or lead the land yields.

children.text: The location's raw material is Silver
The location's raw material is Lead

buildings.name: Breslau Trade Kontor
buildings.text: A merchant trading house in the Hanseatic tradition, channeling the east-west commerce that flows through Breslau's position at the crossroads of the Amber Road and Via Regia.

buildings.name: Sudeten Glass Hut
buildings.text: A glassworks in the mountain forest, of the kind worked at Schreiberhau since 1366. The hut is moved on when the wood around it is burnt.

buildings.name: Church of Peace
buildings.text: A Lutheran church granted by the Peace of Westphalia to a town of Habsburg Silesia: built of timber, clay and straw outside the walls, without tower or bell. It can be raised only where the people follow another faith than their ruler. Its congregation stays quiet, and stays Protestant.

buildings.name: Silesian Protestant Academy
buildings.text: An educational institution born of the Reformation, training clergy, teachers, and civic leaders in Protestant theology and humanist learning.

buildings.name: Silesian Coal Works
buildings.text: An early industrial coal mining operation in Upper Silesia, exploiting the vast deposits that would make the region one of Central Europe's great industrial zones.

where.text: Coal is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Silesian Mechanized Mill
buildings.text: A steam-powered textile factory representing the transformation of Silesian industry from cottage weaving to mechanized production.

buildings.name: Silesian Diplomatic Residence
buildings.text: A palatial residence in the heart of Breslau hosting ambassadors from across Central Europe. This grand building serves as the neutral ground where the affairs of three crowns are settled.

buildings.name: Silesian Trade Hall
buildings.text: A grand commercial exchange where Silesian cloth, minerals, and manufactured goods are traded alongside Baltic commodities. The beating heart of the Central European economy.

list.name: Schlesischer Fürstentag
list.text: The Silesian Princes' Diet, convened at Breslau, gathered the dukes of the cadet Piast and Erbfürsten duchies, the Prince-Bishop of Wrocław, and the deputies of the six royal Silesian cities. The Fürstentag granted taxes, raised the territorial levy, and adjudicated disputes between the duchies. Compared to Bohemia or Saxony, the Silesian estates were unusually fragmented but correspondingly hard for the Bohemian king to coerce. They treated the crown as an external partner and survived as a real check on royal power until Ferdinand II's post-1629 reforms.

list.name: Schlesisches Oberamt
list.text: The Bohemian crown's chief office in Silesia, headed by the Oberlandeshauptmann at Wrocław. The first holder, Bishop Konrad of Oels, was appointed on 16 April 1422 by King Sigismund to organize the defence against the Hussites. Under Matthias Corvinus the office became permanent in 1474, outranking the territorial governors of the duchies and exercising voluntary jurisdiction over the princes. After 1629 Emperor Ferdinand II transformed the Oberamt from a representative body into a purely imperial bureaucracy and the principal instrument of Habsburg centralization in Silesia.

list.name: Bistum Breslau
list.text: The Prince-Bishopric of Wrocław as a temporal polity. Bishop Jaroslaw of Opole received Nysa from his father Bolesław I in 1198; in 1290 Duke Henryk IV confirmed the bishop's sovereignty over Nysa and Ottmachau, and Bishop Przecław of Pogorzela bought the Duchy of Grodków in 1342. Thereafter the bishops of Breslau ruled the Duchy of Nysa-Grodków in their own right, took precedence over the other Silesian rulers, and ran the Catholic-school network that anchored the province against Lutheran encroachment from neighbouring Saxony and Bohemia.

list.name: Tarnowitzer Bergordnung
list.text: The mining code of Upper Silesia. Galena (silver-bearing lead ore) was discovered at Tarnowice around 1490; in 1526 Duke Jan II of Opole and Margrave George of Brandenburg-Ansbach issued the Akt Wolności Górniczej granting Bergfreiheit, and in 1528 the Ordunek Górny codified the rights of free miners, ore shares, and shift discipline. By the mid-16th century Tarnowskie Góry was the largest ore centre in East-Central Europe (some seven thousand staple pits and seven drainage adits), drawing miners from across the Empire and turning Upper Silesia into a Habsburg fiscal asset that survived intact until Frederick II's conquest in 1742.

list.name: Schlesische Erbfürstentümer
list.text: The hereditary Piast cadet duchies. Following the Testament of Bolesław III in 1138, Silesia was partitioned among the descendants of Władysław II the Exile and progressively splintered into Liegnitz, Brieg, Schweidnitz-Jauer, Glogau, Sagan, Münsterberg-Oels, Teschen and a dozen lesser principalities. Each duchy retained its own ducal court and household administration; the last Silesian Piast, George William of Liegnitz, died in 1675. The system multiplied noble offices and produced a civil-law tradition richer than centralized German principalities, but it also fragmented sovereignty in a way the Bohemian crown spent three centuries trying to reverse.
